title: On Measuring Faithfulness or Self-consistency of Natural Language Explanations
authors: Letitia Parcalabescu; Anette Frank
venue: Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers)
evidence_grade: F: primary full-text audit
access_depth: Full-text methods, evaluation, limitations and relevant appendices inspected; no reproduction
contribution: CC-SHAP compares input-token contribution vectors for the answer and the generated explanation. SHAP contribution ratios are signed and normalized by the absolute-sum of input contributions for each generated token; ratios are averaged across output tokens. Final CC-SHAP is one minus cosine distance, i.e. cosine similarity, between the resulting prediction and explanation vectors. This avoids specially crafted editing-test inputs but SHAP itself still evaluates masked coalitions. The authors explicitly call the construct self-consistency, not established internal faithfulness.
limitations: A graded output/input-contribution consistency score is not mechanistic ground truth. Results depend on SHAP masking, Monte Carlo approximation, aggregation and normalization. Very small contributions in long outputs require special handling (Appendix A.3). Requires repeated inference and next-token logits/probabilities, but not gradients or activation access. Authors report about four minutes/example for CC-SHAP and six–36 hours per model/task for the full test suite; these are paper-specific runtimes. English-only autoregressive experiments; model-size relationship not established. Human judgment cannot establish unknown internal reasoning, although humans can judge other defined evidence-consistency properties.
relevance: A consistency benchmark, contribution-profile comparison and comparison of multiple faithfulness tests are established prior art. Any G1/G2 proposal should distinguish semantic supported-claim preservation from attribution-profile similarity. Do not claim that a checker score establishes complete internal faithfulness.
baseline_use: Suitable as an optional per-instance consistency diagnostic when target-model probabilities and enough repeated inference are available. Expensive to run across every candidate and audience variant. Black-box text-only APIs without probability access cannot directly support the released metric. A simplified alternative must be labelled an adaptation.

title: A Necessary Step toward Faithfulness: Measuring and Improving Consistency in Free-Text Explanations
authors: Lingjun Zhao; Hal Daumé III
venue: Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
evidence_grade: F: primary full-text audit
access_depth: Full-text methods, evaluation, limitations and relevant appendices inspected; no reproduction
contribution: PEX consistency measures how an explanation favors a prediction over its negation. Although the original definition is a sequence-likelihood ratio, experiments use adjusted PEX (Eq4): posterior label log-odds with explanation appended minus prior label log-odds without it. Models are first supervised-fine-tuned for binary opinion-spam classification; sampled explanations are ranked by PEX to construct preference pairs, then DPO trains the explanation model. Evaluation trains student models to simulate teacher predictions, using teacher explanations during student training but not at test time.

PEX is a contrastive support/consistency construct, not semantic proof that all prose claims are supported by the original input or that latent reasoning is accurately exposed. Experiments are binary classification; multiclass extension is future work. The simulation endpoint is system-level, not an individual explanation verification certificate, and assumes simulation is a useful proxy. SFT/DPO and student training impose substantial compute. Authors report SFT/DPO on one RTX A6000 for roughly 24 h per described training configuration; student training 1–2 h. Qualitative examples and average PEX do not establish all outputs are consistent.
